assignat-1790s.title: Assignat
hits: On 21 December 1789 a first decree was voted through, ordering the issue (in April 1790) of 400,000 livres' worth of assignats, certificates of indebtedness, with an interest rate of 5%, secured and repayable based on the auctioning of the "Biens nationaux".
On 17 April 1790, the notes were declared legal tender but their interest was reduced to 3%.
For daily life smaller denominations of 200 and 300 livres were needed.
As soon as the assignats started to circulate, their value decreased by 5 percent.
On 27 August 1790 the Assembly decided another issue of 1,9 billion assignats which would become legal tender before the end of the year for all actions, c.q.
The massive and dangerous issue of 1,9 billion he succeeded to get down to 800 million, but the attacks may have influenced his resignation.

On 29 September 1790, the National Assembly authorized a further issue of 800 million livres and abolished interest on the assignats altogether.)
Necker foretold that the paper money, with which the dividends were about to be paid, would soon be of no value.

By September 1790, the assignat had become a true circulating paper currency, and 800 million livres worth of non-interest bearing notes were added to the initial issue, in denominations of 50, 60 70, 80, 90, 100, 500, and 2000 livres with legal-tender status.

continental-currency-1775.title: Early American currency
hits: Continental currency was denominated in dollars from $1⁄6 to $80, including many odd denominations in between.
During the Revolution, Congress issued $199,990,000 in Continental currency.
In the 1790s, after the ratification of the United States Constitution, Continentals could be exchanged for treasury bonds at 1% of face value.
Morris helped finance the final stages of the war by issuing notes in his name, backed by his personal line of credit, which was further backed by a French loan of $450,000 in silver coins.
